There is something that gnostic thought shares with Hinduism. It's probably the case that this vector originated with the Hindus and came into Gnosticism through Pythagoreanism in Greece and Plato's elaboration on this chain-of-being cosmology, which trickled into the mixed milieu of ancient Palestine. Once there, this Hellenistic cosmology co-mingled with Judaism and Egyptian thinking (via Alexandria) to set the stage for Gnosticism. Roughly, we get from both Egyptians and Greek mystery schools a focus on inner knowledge and the crucial force of the individual inward journey as the path to salvation. Know thyself. From the Jews enters Mosaic monotheism. The emanationist cosmology seems to have its primordial birth with Hinduism, but its rational elaboration through Plato and later Jewish mystics. Gnosticism arose in this ferment, from what I consider to be a great moral effort to understand our predicament of being-in-the-world. How should we understand the moral status of the material world, generally?

The heterogeneous syncretism in this important part of the world (really, foundational for the future of mankind) makes it clear why a figure like Christ could be interpreted in such varied ways. Gnosticism itself isn't a term which the people we reference by using it would have ever called themselves. It would only be later, as histories were being dictated and broad polemics were being issued against the Gnostics, that we get the elaboration of sectarian names for the different Gnostic groups.

There is one crucial philosophical idea held commonly by the Hindus and the Gnostics, and only in its broadest sense, which is the rejection of the material world. This isn't to say that either group sought to reduce or eliminate all moral significance for the goings on in the world. Rather, insofar as this rejection represented a general dismissal of the eternal significance of this world, it was a rejection of absolute meaning in the material. Perhaps the better way to describe this rejection would be to say that the infinite (eternal) and the finite (mortal) aspects of reality are related in the way that truth and falsehood are related, respectively. For Hinduism there is Maya and a sort of trickery played by God on itself: the one consciousness instantiates the persona, a mask about which it must be the task of every so-called person to dissolve (by way of inward reflection on one's true identity with Brahman).

The Gnostics (probably from the influence of Judaism and Zoroaster) attached malevolence to the falsehood of reality. For them, we are not here as part of an ultimately trifling performance. Instead, we are here because malevolent emanations of God imprisoned us here, trapping the divine spark of our source inside material bodies. The relatedness is clear, but these two worldviews have a completely different affect and, therefore, a totally different psychology.

Orthodox Judaism and Christianity did something very different in terms of situating humans within creation. From the beginning they internalized the antagonism between themselves and the one true God by positing The Fall, which localized the misfortune of existence to man himself. This isn't a stage play in which we can causally discharge evil as an artifact of selfish acts like the Hindus might suggest. Nor is it a result of pure malevolence by an angry demiurge. Instead, we get sin as a great target-missing on the part of man. For whatever criticisms may be levied against it, having to do with the autonomous guilt this delegates to every person (even before they've had a chance to do evil), the human effect which I am interested in is both theological and psychological.

In terms of theology, and representing an important point of divergence with the Jews, the Christians came to understand the coming Kingdom as a kingdom of the spirit, a more or less conscious and moral state of global Christ likeness. Contrast this with the more ancient Jewish prophecies which speak of a physical, geopolitically situated kingdom. Instead, with the Christians we get the idea of the Church, fully extricating the act of preparing the Kingdom from politics and placing it in the realm of the spirit. This also implicates every Christian person with the inherent life-mission to evangelize in the spirit. The Jews saw the world as fallen, always in a catastrophic descent towards apocalypse, requiring the advent of a savior to install God's literal kingdom on Earth. The Christian, on the other hand, views creation as something more like a moral and military theater, having all of the significance of a proving ground for the very purification of fallen souls to secure their eternal existence in a heavenly kingdom (as opposed to the salty messianism of the Jews).

Both Judaism and Christianity, then, gain a fundamentally more urgent significance for the material world. I made it a point above to highlight that the Christian Church is (in the most symbolic sense) a unification of a people within the spirit. However, its significance for moral action in the world cannot be decoupled from the meaning of institutional church-building. The Christians, with an eye on eternity, cannot forego the profound importance of this short-lived material existence.

Where the Hindu doesn't altogether reduce the relevance of existence according to the law of karma, I find that they are also far less compelled to engage with the world as though their doing so has cosmic significance. Rather, so long as they do not do evil, their identification directly with the Godhead promotes a kind of 'sleeping in the sun' affect, if not the more respectable asceticism which is still iconic of worldly rejection. Whereas the ideal Christian feels compelled to glorify creation by exalting the senses/body/mind with active engagement in the affairs of the world, the Hindu prioritizes meditative states and going beneath introspection to dwell in a mindless state of oneness. In this there is a rejection of the ego-consciousness, which Christianity exalts and can hardly do without - indeed it exalts the soul and the attached intellect as an image of the God image (not an identity, but an image). This is absolutely crucial to the distinction.

The Gnostics, on the other hand, pursued the ascetic disregard for the material world with, at times, even greater zealousness than the Hindus, pushing the survival of the body and the poverty of lifestyle to the brink - as a means to liberate the divine spark and achieve gnosis. A brief observation of gnostic history in the 1st millennium AD reveals that almost no amount of asceticism and poverty was enough. Schisms within groups were frequent due to infighting about one group's level of engagement with society. It's easy to understand this commitment if we grasp the fundamentality of the evil of material existence in Gnosticism.

Both Hinduism and Gnosticism result in a world bereft of real meaning. In the former, we're confronted by the illusion of individual identity and a world which amounts to little more than a God playing solitaire with itself. In the latter, the only imperative that can be justified logically from one's beliefs is escape: we exist to escape existence.

The Abrahamic faiths are unique in that they add meaning to the material world, by acknowledging that it is a creation intended to be glorified, and one in which we can see beauty - indeed, the world is a grounds for beauty to materialize, and where mankind is situated to act as a sub-creator below God and the hierarchy of angels to add to the beauty and goodness of creation. In fact, he is called to do so. He must. Christianity does not proclaim a need to escape anything here, other than one's own individual scar of sin, and this happens not by way of dismissing the world. We are told in the Bible that we are to live in the world, but not of it.

No incentives are offered to the Christian for escaping our illusion into the depths of meditation, or to consciously pursue poverty as a means of salvation itself - rather, it gives man a meaning and a duty to engage with the world. We are far more like soldiers in this view than passive experiencers of a trick or a psychic prison. The evil does not belong to a demiurge. It belongs to us, and it falls on us to seek expiation via grace. Christ abolished the Mosaic covenant as a self-sacrificial sacrament to impart the possibility for grace to man, but by implicating man in his own salvation (to be worked out in fear and trembling). We aren't here merely to breathe, or to think, or to experience ourselves - we find ourselves in a world where almost everywhere there exists a demand for action, to better the world - along with the revelatory blueprint (in the Christ imago) for just how to go about that.

It's this active principle as opposed to the passivity of other belief systems that makes Christianity so much more attractive to me. All of this contributes to a certain development of beauty in the Christian aesthetic. It's clean and elegant, moreover, it has a reason to be. Dignifying the material is a moral claim in itself, toward realizing the dignity that is potentia in all of it. This exalts the power we have to be creators, to clean up. When getting together with fellow Christians, there's reason to lace up my fucking shoes and press my shirt. No, we aren't going to shit in the street and live in the woods from bugs and honey. We can do better, and we should. This orderliness, which we saw perhaps in Hitler's Germany, is what really speaks to me psychologically.

You are touching on something very important here, but as usual there is something lost in the subtleties, I think. First I'll comment on the error I see, and then on how this ties into the way in which you are profoundly correct.

Christianity has precisely the same ascetic sense, precisely the same emphasis on mortification and self-denial and negation as the other faiths you've named. One need only read the Meister on "negating the negation" (negating everything in us that is not God); or St. John of the Cross on the Dark Night of the Soul, and how one becomes more conscious of these negations within us that require negating as we grow in holiness; or St Therese of Liseaux (the Little Flower) and her intense desire to be mortified for the Lord; or St Theresa of Avila, and her Interior Castle, her "levels" of self-purgation; etc. etc., to see how this is so. It is central to the Christian faith that nothing unclean, nothing unpurified, can enter the Kingdom of heaven, and anything that remains any degree of attachment to a creature whatsoever is unclear in the sight of the Lord. This is why Purgatory is essential, since without it only the very few who become saints in this life and have progressed through the levels of the Interior Castle, who have endured the dark night of the soul, could possibly enter into the heavenly Kingdom.

So this renouncement, this detachment, is not just a part of Christianity, but is integral to it. Christianity shares this with the other faiths; this attitude is common among them because it is true.

However (and thus is what you have correctly identified, I think), the difference is that, while the truth of Hinduism or Gnosticism is limited to its esoteric level of understanding, the truth of Christianity is fully manifested both at the esoteric and exoteric level. The monkeys, tree, and elephant gods of the Orient are merely symbolic of the esoteric truths to which they point. Jesus Christ, and likewise His sacraments, on the other hand, are both symbolic and real even at the exoteric level. It is this reality, this fullness of Truth within the Christian faith that enables a respect, even a certain reverence, for the creation, for the person. So for the Hindu or the Gnostic, nothing but the End itself may be seen as meaningful, and so anything to do with the material, the phenomenal, the corporeal, is to be dismissed (by the aspirant holy man, anyway) as illusory, as not worth consideration. Thus you don't get great works of art, great sciences and technological feats, great symphonies and chants and structures, except in defiance of this aacription of illusion to the material. Christianity, however, even though it too seeks to negate all attachment to the emanations, to the creatures, insofar as they are taken to be something in themselves, still cannot help but see these things as profoundly meaningful, even important, because inseparable from Christian doctrine is the exoteric teaching. It is not the Logos that was crucified, but Christ in His humanity as well as His Divinity. It is not some ethereal light that redeemed humanity, but the Blood of Christ. It is not a divine whisoer that brings us into the Church, but the water of sacramental baptism. Man is both body and soul, both matter and form, and so we as Christians must recognize our nature as partly corporeal, and therefore the role that the corporeal must play in our salvation, while simultaneously seeing that the corporeal is meaningful only as a means, not as an end, and that our end is in fact to escape any attachment to the corporeal as corporeal, to the creaturely as creaturely, and instead fix our eyes on God alone.
